Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
Being emotionally close or intimate with others
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette:
Liam Weber was a 32-year-old tutor who came to treatment exhausted, ashamed of how much smaller his life had become, and frightened by how quickly ordinary moments could turn menacing. The stalking had begun almost a year earlier after he had ended several sessions with an adult student who had become increasingly intrusive. At first it was unsettling rather than terrifying: repeated messages from new numbers, long emails that mixed apology with accusation, sightings of the same motorcycle idling across from his apartment building. What made it feel unmistakably dangerous was the persistence. He began noticing the rider outside the tutoring center where he worked, then near the grocery store, then behind him when he took a different route home. One evening he looked over his shoulder and saw the bike slow when he slowed. By the time he reached his building, his hands were shaking so badly he dropped his keys. After that, the sound of a motorcycle engine no longer registered as traffic; it landed in his body as proof that he had been found again.

In the weeks that followed, Liam became preoccupied with the idea that people were never what they seemed. The stalking had convinced him that a person could present as needy, polite, even calm, while hiding something coercive underneath. He had come to mistrust others broadly, and he doubted his own judgment most of all. He replayed early interactions with the student and was certain he should have recognized the danger sooner, should have said something different, should have done the right thing before it escalated. That self-doubt sharpened the force of his triggers. If he heard even mild anger in someone's voice-a parent objecting to a scheduling issue, a stranger snapping at a cashier-his mind moved immediately to hidden menace. The controlled tone frightened him almost more than shouting; to Liam, calm anger meant someone was masking intention. Likewise, the sensation of being followed no longer needed much evidence. A pedestrian behind him for half a block or a car slowing near the curb could be enough to activate the belief that appearances were deceptive and that he could not trust himself to judge danger accurately.

Those beliefs gradually shaped how he lived. Because he no longer trusted other people's motives, and because he was not sure he would make good decisions if something happened again, he started keeping emotional distance from his wife. He told himself he was protecting her from his tension, but privately he also felt he deserved to suffer and should not be comforted. When she reached for him at night, he would go still or pretend to be tired. He also stopped letting himself relax in any real way. If he noticed his body softening while watching television or sitting beside her on the couch, he would tense again, as if dropping his guard invited danger. In his mind, closeness and relaxation meant vulnerability, and vulnerability was exactly how people got hurt without seeing it coming.

That way of coping left him increasingly keyed up. Nights became especially difficult. He had trouble falling asleep and, when he did sleep, woke at small sounds and lay listening for an engine outside. Because he spent so much energy braced against comfort and held himself apart from the one person who might have soothed him, his sense of danger rarely came down. False alarms became common. He would jerk around in public, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that someone had stepped too close behind him. The more frequently this happened, the more potent the triggers became. A motorcycle passing the tutoring center could undo an entire afternoon. If he heard raised irritation in the hallway before a lesson, he found himself scanning faces, trying to determine who was hiding something. He began avoiding unfamiliar places altogether because not knowing the exits, the parking layout, or who might be waiting there felt intolerable. His world narrowed to routes he had memorized and rooms where he could keep the door in view.

This had begun to affect his work. As a tutor, he often met students in libraries, homes, and learning centers, but now he pushed for online sessions or refused new locations outright. If a student's parent expressed annoyance, even calmly, he struggled to stay focused on the material; part of him was already tracking tone, posture, and whether anyone else was in the building. On bad days he felt followed walking from his car to the center, and once inside he checked the windows for motorcycles before he could begin teaching. He knew these reactions sounded excessive when he described them, yet he was equally certain that people could not be trusted and that his own instincts had failed him before.

By the time he sought help, Liam was sleeping poorly, avoiding much of the city, and living with his wife more like a guarded roommate than a partner. What finally brought him in was an evening when she asked, not angrily but with obvious hurt, whether he was ever really with her anymore, and he felt the same jolt of alarm he felt with any trace of emotion in another person's voice. He was frightened that this was becoming permanent-that he would keep mistaking ordinary life for danger, keep punishing himself, and keep withdrawing from the people he loved. More than anything, he wanted to be able to hear a motorcycle, or someone speaking sharply, or footsteps behind him, without feeling as though the stalking were happening all over again.
